subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His predecessor was quite right. Last year,
330,000	new jobs were created.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have continued unemployment at 6 per cent.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This year should be better.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what you have been saying for four years.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has gotten better in every one of those four years. We have a continuous rise in the economy of Canada over a fairly long period. The budget of the Minister of Finance will continue the expansion that is now under way. In Canada, we have a very rapidly and steadily expanding economy. The opposition is trying to say that we are not expanding. The evidence is to be seen on all sides. It is to be found in all the figures that appear every month that there is a very rapid expansion of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is your last budget speech.
The Budget-Mr. Sharp

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Whether that very substantial increase in the number of jobs will reduce the level of unemployment is another question. As the Minister of Finance said, it probably will. However, here in Canada we are going through a most extraordinary period of expansion in the labour force. There is nothing like it anywhere else in the world. If our labour force were stable, as it is in continental Europe today, we would have more than full employment. However, we do not. These are not the conditions we face. We face the most rapidly increasing labour force in the world. The growth in employment in Canada last year was far greater than that of virtually any other industrial nation, and four times the percentage increase in employment in the United States, but we still had unemployment.
We are all concerned about those who, notwithstanding the buoyancy of the economy and the increase in jobs, cannot find work immediately. That is why the government improved the terms of unemployment insurance, embarked upon enlarged programs of manpower training, introduced the Local Initiatives Program and Opportunities for Youth which have been such a resounding success. However, let us not confuse this concern about the unemployed with silly statements that the Canadian government is faltering and that the government is failing to give sufficient stimulus. In fact, we are one of the most rapidly expanding countries, if not the most rapidly expanding in the world.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I join with others in congratulating the Minister of Finance for including in his budget message relief for those unable to keep pace with rising prices; the elderly retired, the disabled and the veterans.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The time has come to incorporate into these basic pensions an automatic adjustment to rising living costs. Such automatic adjustments involve a certain risk. This has been recognized over a period of years. However, in my judgment and the judgment of the government, this is a risk that must be accepted. By this action, by increasing the Guaranteed Income Supplement by $15 per month and by raising the exemptions for the elderly, Canada has maintained its reputation as the most generous country in the world in its treatment of veterans, pensioners and the disabled.
May I add one further thought by way of conclusion, Mr. Speaker. It is because over the years Canada has followed a responsible fiscal and monetary policy and because our economic performance has been so satisfactory that we can afford to have this deserved reputation for humanitarianism.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, Hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will continue to follow the nonpartisan path the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has established. I do not intend to run the great risk of dislocating my shoulder by slapping myself on the back as often as the minister did.
In the course of what I have to say today, I intend to address myself mainly to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and his budget remarks. I do not propose to argue

May 15, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
with him today as to whether or not it is a responsible budget, as far as it goes. I am more concerned, as the minister should be, about whether this budget is truly responsive to the needs of the country at this time. Applying that test, I find there are many significant ways in which the budget falls short of being satisfactory. These areas of shortfall are outlined in the amendment introduced in the House by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
In speaking to that amendment today, I wish to cover several of those areas of the budget in which the proposals cannot be considered realistically responsive. There is one basic fact about the Canadian economy, despite all the palaver of the Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon. In the past two years or so, our economy has been running below its potential at the rate of about $3 billion a year. The unemployment arising from this situation constitutes the principal challenge which faces the government in 1972. The gap is a real gap. It is not just a matter of statistics. It is certainly real for more than
600,000	Canadians who are out of work and looking for jobs; it is real for the taxpayer who is shelling out to meet the costs of welfare payments arising from unemployment; it is real for businessmen looking for sales and it is real for every man, woman and child who is in some way bearing the burden of an economy which is not producing to its full potential.
I do not propose to dwell on the fact that this gap was deliberately created by the present government. That is common knowledge; there is no reason for me to elaborate on it. But having created this situation, one would almost believe that the government was determined to preserve this gap between the rate at which the economy is operating and the rate at which it should be operating to provide something like an acceptable standard of employment. I have heard of people falling in love with their own mistakes. That is about the only explanation I can give for the seeming determination of the government to do almost anything rather than get the economy moving again at the rate required to narrow the gap rapidly and regain an employment situation which any civilized country would wish to achieve.
So, the first priority of the government must be to get rid of the gap between the actual and the potential operation of the economy. In concrete terms, this means a vigorous and determined effort to create enough jobs to get rid of the shameful phenomenon of mass unemployment which has existed in this country for some time. This is the measuring rod against which we must judge the budgetary measures the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has proposed. The budget we are considering today is the first budget which the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) has placed before the House. Appropriately enough, it has, superficially, a new look.
I had been hoping the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) would stay with us. He might learn something in passing.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will be back.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Something non-partisan. As I was saying, there is, superficially, a new look about some of the measures the minister has proposed, at least by comparison with other budgets I have heard presented in the House. There is a modicum of justice done to some of our pensioners, though the move has come rather late in the day. I must say that if this step is followed by an immediate election the minister will have shown himself to possess a degree of political cynicism I did not think he had. Further, the fact that about 700,000 pensioners will benefit to the tune of some $2.88 a month is a reminder that the government still knows how to be petty. These pensioners, who have been bearing the brunt of inflation ever since January 1, 1967, should have been awarded an increase in their basic pension sufficient to compensate them adequately for the deterioration in purchasing power which has taken place since the last major change late in 1966. This would involve an adjustment, not of $2.88 but of nearly $15 a month in the basic pension. I have no hesitation in saying that the government I expect to lead shortly will do just that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us examine the methods the minister has used in his budget to stimulate the economy. There is, of course, the reduction the minister proposes in the rate of corporate tax affecting firms in the manufacturing and processing industries effective January 1 next year. Then, there is the provision for fast write-offs affecting some firms who buy new equipment, effective immediately. This is another aspect of the new look. There is a sort of industrial strategy involved here. That is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs was trying to say this afternoon.
The Minister of Finance is proposing to reduce corporate taxes as they affect certain firms. Revenue loss, as a result, will be supplied by raising personal income tax and, to some extent, increasing the taxes levied on other corporations. Last October all corporate taxes were reduced for a period of 18 months. This will cease to be the case at the end of 1972.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was dealt with by parliament.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is the 1972 year. I was merely pointing out that the reduction in taxes which the minister proposes in order to assist certain firms who engage in manufacturing and processing constitutes, in effect, a transfer which is bound to increase the load carried by individual taxpayers and other types of corporations. Personal income tax rates will go up 3 per cent on January 1. The minister did not call attention to this, but it is undeniable that they will go up.
Furthermore, the very fact that inflation is taking place at the rate of about 5 per cent per annum does, in itself, mean that the rate of taxation on personal income is increasing and will continue to increase, because inflation, applied to a progressive tax schedule, automatically means that if there is a 5 per cent increase in personal income the government will get much more than a 5 per cent increase in tax. So, while the minister is proposing this cut in taxation affecting certain kinds of corpora-
May 15, 1972

tions, let us bear in mind that taxes paid by other corporations will increase and, of course, taxes on personal income will increase. They will increase, first of all, because they are being put up expressly, and, second, because the process of inflation applied to the progressive income tax schedule automatically means that a person who does not get a nickel more in terms of real income in 1972 than in 1971 will be obliged to pay a great deal more to the government in proportion to that real income.
We have personal income taxes going up for two reasons. We have, as I say, a transfer of tax from certain types of corporations to personal income tax payers and, to some extent, to corporations. We have a new national policy which is a subsidy. I do not want the minister to get upset, as I am not criticizing his policy, I am just explaining what it is. It is a subsidy on the exports of those firms which can benefit from the minister's proposal, and a subsidy also toward the domestic sales of these firms which can comply. In other words, it does involve a form of protection. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) can say he does not believe in tariffs or protection, but the minister is in fact applying a form of protection to companies which can qualify.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a pretty farfetched economic argument.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is perfectly true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am just explaining what the situation is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You don't understand your own budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What the minister is doing is providing a subsidy through tax transfers for these companies in respect of domestic sales and, to some extent, in respect of exports. This is a national policy to encourage manufacturing in this country in order to increase our share of the domestic market, and to increase opportunities in the export area. The minister should be prepared to call it what it is.
I am not describing this move in these terms for the purpose of criticizing what the minister is proposing to do. I am not criticizing it as such. I am attempting to show what is being done. I am not objecting to this sort of encouragement being given to manufacturing and processing concerns, because I believe it will help them to be more competitive in the world as it actually exists. I have been for some time emphasizing the importance of Canadian corporations being able to compete in the world as it is. I have said that, and I welcome what the minister has done, provided it is accompanied by some other measures.
What measures should accompany the help the minister is proposing for certain corporations in this country? The purpose he has in mind is to create jobs in manufacturing and processing industries. His measure would only do so where there is an additional market available at home or abroad to these firms. I must say I found the Secretary of State for External Affairs extraordinarily complacent this afternoon in view of the marketing problems and the questions of access to markets that a country such as
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
Canada faces today. He talked about these problems, but exhibited an extraordinary degree of complacency about them.
The Minister of Finance assumes that the encouragement he has offered will enable Canadian manufacturing and processing industries to get a bigger share of either the foreign market or the domestic market, presumably by reducing prices. Presumably that is what the minister has in mind, that these firms will be able to reduce their prices and be more competitive. Some of these firms will be able to do so to an unpredictable extent. The minister has said it will be some years before we really know the results of what he has proposed. In other words, he is not putting something before this House which will result in any dramatic increase in employment. As he says himself, this is something that may take years to have any real effect. The firms that will get any help from what the minister is proposing are those firms that are now making money and earning income. A very substantial percentage of firms are losing money, frequently because of competitive marketing conditions and not through inefficiency, and I point out to the minister that this proposal offers no help at all to them. The minister cannot deny that.
Furthermore, and far more important, his proposal is virtually useless to new industry. His proposal is of very little ecouragement to anybody or any group wanting to start a new industry in this country because, generally speaking, a new industry does not have any net income for many years. I say in all earnestness to the minister that what he is proposing, even for manufacturing and processing industries, will be of very, very little encouragement to the commencement of new industries in this area in Canada. If we are going to really succeed in fighting unemployment and creating the employment we want in the manufacturing and processing industries in this country we have to start a lot of new industries, and I say to the minister that his proposal is of no consequence at all in that regard.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a silly statement.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I beg your pardon.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I say, that is surely not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister says that is not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How do you help a company that has no income to tax?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is all very well for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to say that is a silly statement, but it is a statement he cannot challenge because it is absolutely correct. A reduction in corporation tax and a fast writeoff offers virtually no encouragement to people to commence new industries because they cannot get any benefit from those proposals for years to come.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is absolutely correct.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I repeat, that is a silly statement.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am afraid the Secretary of State for External Affairs does not understand these things.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, I do, very well.

May 15, 1972
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He used to have these troubles when he was Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think you should get new research men.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is obvious why we have a different Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these gentlemen ought to consult some people who know something about this. If they consult people who are interested in starting new businesses they will find that what I have said is absolutely correct. I will return to the subject, Mr. Speaker.
I am simply pointing out now that the proposal of the minister falls far short of being an effective tool to expand Canadian manufacturing and processing. I also point out that there is really nothing here to encourage Canadians to invest more of their money in their economy in order to play a bigger part in the ownership of that Canadian economy in the future. I also point out to the Minister of Finance that, in so far as he claims that reducing these taxes will make these corporations more profitable, this is just as attractive to foreign capital as it is to Canadian capital. There is nothing in the minister's proposal which encourages Canadians as such to acquire a bigger share of the economy in the future.
If the Minister of Finance refers to the dividend credit that is available in connection with personal income taxes, I agree that encourages Canadians to invest their money in shares and to establish dividend paying corporations. It provides little if any encouragement, however, to Canadians to invest their money in risk enterprises or in new enterprises which will not pay dividends for years. That kind of incentive was not given before, and it is not provided in the minister's budget.
I have already said I accept the principle of the proposal made by the government to screen takeovers. I want the Secretary of State for External Affairs to hear me on this because a minute ago he misquoted me. I repeat for the benefit of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, so that he will know my view on this subject and not misinterpret it, that I accept the principle of the proposal to screen takeovers as made by the government, but I also say that this will not in itself increase the Canadian role in our economy, and I do not think the government seriously suggests it will. It may prevent certain takeovers and enable Canada to obtain a better deal in respect of certain other takeovers, but it will not increase Canadian participation in our economy. That can be done by positive measures and there are no such positive measures in the budget.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Such as?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister says "such as". I will come to that. In view of the time I am taking, the minister may have to wait for the second exciting instalment of my budget speech. The question of encouraging Canadians to participate in the economy is closely related to the failure of the minister to encourage the development of new manufacturing and processing enterprises in Canada. As I have said, I intend to return to this whole subject.
What are the other weaknesses in the budget proposals? The Minister of Finance says he has decided there is enough stimulus in the economy, after allowing for the increase in pensions which is the only increase on the demand side the minister proposes. The minister said there is enough disposable income available. He is concerned that if the disposable income were increased a lot of it would be spent on imports. The Secretary of State for External Affairs this afternoon spoke about leakage. I would hate to set myself up in competition with any member of this government when it comes to leakage. Of course, some of this money would be spent on imports. It always is. However, a very large proportion of it would also be spent in Canada. There is plenty of room for increasing output in Canada with the spare capacity and with 6 per cent of the labour force unemployed. Personal income taxes were not reduced. In fact, as I indicated, they are actually being increased in two ways. The actual increase of 3 per cent is taking place and there is the implicit increase which takes place through inflation as applied to our graduated scale of income tax. Yet, while the minister will not stimulate the economy in this way, he projects a rate of growth of the Canadian economy which involves the continuation of massive unemployment in this country for years to come, according to his own projections.
The other day I gave the minister the opportunity to dissasociate himself with the projections of the Economic Council of Canada concerning the real rate of growth required in Canada to bring unemployment down to around 4 per cent even over a period of two or three years. The minister did not disassociate himself from that forecast. Yet, his forecast of the rate of growth is substantially below the rate of growth the Economic Council of Canada says is necessary in order to bring unemployment down to even 4 per cent over two or three years. It is all very well for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to talk about the growth in the work force. Of course, we have a rapidly growing work force. The Economic Council of Canada pointed that out as far back as 1965. There is nothing new about this. That is the great reason the decision taken in 1969 by that minister and his colleagues to deliberately slow down the economy has involved us in tragedy. It is the reason we are having such difficulty now, and it is the reason it is such a crime to have this complacent government in a position of responsibility today. The Minister of Finance and his colleagues have accepted the continuance of high unemployment in this country for years to come, and that involves waste, the destruction of morale, a cost to the taxpayers and everything which goes with this situation. Why has he accepted it?	;
Why has the minister, in May 1972, adopted a less expansionist budget than his predecessor adopted in June a year ago or as recently as October last? Is he afraid of being charged with buying votes? The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested he did not want to run the risk of being so charged. That did not prevent the increases in old age pensions, and of course it should not have.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not buying votes, I hope.

May 15, 1972

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Exactly. The government should not be open to that charge because everybody on this side of the House urged the minister to increase old age pensions. So far as reducing taxes are concerned, the minister was in exactly the same position. Everybody on this side of the House was urging this and suggesting it was desirable. No one over here could accuse the Minister of Finance of seeking votes by reducing personal income tax because we were all saying this was desirable.
Was it because of a fear of inflation that the minister did not reduce personal income tax. Is that the reason the Minister of Finance allowed the personal income tax to rise substantially in the course of the current fiscal year? Was it because of a fear of inflation? It is my conviction that an increase in employment is our number one social priority. Unemployment must be reduced. I say that even if in our effort to cut it down in a humane manner inflation should escalate, then we will deal with it even if we must impose temporary controls. Let us deal with unemployment in a humane way. The government and the minister continue to run the economy below its potential as an anti-inflationary measure to curb inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said he would not hesitate to do again what he did in 1969 and 1970 to fight inflation by slowing down the economy and creating massive unemployment. One can see this attitude reflected in the budget the minister presented. This government still expects the pensioners and the unemployed to be the sacrificial goats in its efforts to control inflation. I won't buy it.
I say that a rate of unemployment of 6 per cent or 5 per cent is inhumane, is uncivilized and is unCanadian. So, I totally reject the minister's approach of maintaining high unemployment as a method of containing inflation. I think it is pretty silly anyway to talk about the risk of overheating an economy which has an idle plant and a seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment of 6 per cent. We are a long distance from having an overheated economy.
What reason is there to believe that the government's reluctance to reduce personal income taxes-in fact, the government's actual increase in personal income taxes- will reduce the inflationary forces which work in this country today? I do not think that the people of this country are fools. They know when they are paying more taxes, and they know that they will be paying more personal taxes under the minister's budget. Will this encourage restraint in wage and salary demands in this country? Will the minister's budget seem equitable and fair to the ordinary Canadian? A reduction in personal income taxes was needed to prevent the tax on real incomes from rising, in other words a reduction in rates was required to prevent income taxes from rising in the circumstances. But a reduction in personal income taxes in association with the corporate tax cuts would, in my judgment, encourage restraint. The national policy of the minister to cut the taxes of corporations associated with something that would seem fair to the individual taxpayer would, in my judgment, have encouraged restraint and not have fed the fires of inflation.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
I suggest that the minister is asking too much of the ordinary Canadian. At least he should not have added to his personal income taxes, at least he should have given him some consideration and provided some real stimulation to the Canadian economy at the same time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we are to have restraint, we have to have fairness. I am concerned about several aspects of inflation. Unemployment being created and endured in the name of inflation is one aspect that concerns me, and like everybody else in the House I am concerned about the burden that inflation imposes on Canadians with fixed incomes. I am particularly concerned that the government of Canada has a vested interest in inflation. The reason for that is very simple. The graduated structure of tax rates under which we operate means that every jump in money income puts progressively more money in the coffers of this government through personal income taxes. It means, for example, that a rate of inflation of 5 per cent in a year increases government revenues by amounts considerably in excess of 5 per cent. It means that a taxpayer whose income simply keeps abreast of rising prices, without improving his position at all in terms of real income, is paying more money to the government of Canada under existing circumstances, and it means that without having taken any initiative of its own the government of Canada is increasing its revenues at the expense of the taxpayer. As the individual citizen gets poor, this government grows rich.
I am aware of the fact that the Carter Commission rejected any efforts to tax only the real increase in personal income. But the position taken by the Carter Commission was taken in the context of a rate of inflation substantially less than 2 per cent a year during the previous five years. I say that today we operate in a context which is totally different, one where annual rates of inflation are 4 per cent or 5 per cent, involving and requiring different measures than in the days of the Carter Commission and the modest inflation which existed then.
I say that if the government of Canada is sincere about fighting inflation, if it is sincere about justice, if it is sincere about honesty and fair dealing with the people it is serving, there is only one thing it can do, and that is get rid of its own vested interest in inflation which it can do in one, simple effective way. What I propose and what a government that I lead will do, is henceforth to calculate personal net income for federal tax purposes in constant dollars.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The appropriate base year for this calculation would be the year 1971, the year of the so-called tax reform, the year in which the government put through the House a rate schedule which it said was fair and equitable. The constant dollar calculation would be achieved by employing a consumer price index factor made available by Canada Statistics and shown on the income tax forms for the year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would you also control your expenditures in constant dollars?

The Budget-Mr. Stanfield

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will come to that in a minute. That is another advantage in what I am proposing. It would be a simple calculation for the taxpayer, and there is no difficult administrative problem for the Department of National Revenue. If the cost of living in any year has increased by 10 per cent above 1971, then the income for tax purposes would be reduced by that percentage. That involves a very simple calculation. This would produce tax payable in 1971 dollars. Another very simple calculation would convert that figure back into the current dollars of the year to indicate the amount of tax available in the dollars of the year in question.
As of the inception of the so-called tax reform, schedules of personal income tax rates and exemptions were fixed for an indefinite period in the future. Under my proposal, these ongoing schedules would relate to ongoing real income rather than to inflated cash income. Thus, the federal tax payable would be free from any inflationary component so far as personal income tax is concerned. This would be just for the taxpayer, and it would force any government to come out into the open. If the government needed a bigger share of personal income to finance its operations, it would have to come before parliament and seek an increase in rates rather than relying, as it now does, on inflation to do its dirty work for it. The government can no longer count on inflation through graduated income tax rates to provide it automatically with a bigger and bigger share of the real income of taxpayers and a bigger and bigger share of the gross national product.
This proposal would be fair to the taxpayer. If his real income rises through the years, he will pay more income tax in real terms, but if he does no more than keep pace with the rise in the cost of living, he would not be penalized; he would pay the same rate as before. It is a simple proposal to calculate income taxes in any year by computing personal income in that year in 1971 dollars. It is a simple proposal but, as the minister realizes, one with tremendous implications. First of all, it would protect citizens from tax increases imposed upon them by inflation rather than imposed upon them as a result of an increase in their real income.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It doesn't. It just changes the tax rates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You don't understand it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs that centuries ago parliament fought the king for the right to control taxation. It achieved that control. But in recent years, that control has been very largely eroded through the ability of the government to increase tax rates in fact without changing the schedules, as a result of inflation. The steady inflation we have had for years has emasculated parliamentary control over taxation. My proposal would restore the fundamental principle of parliamentary control over the rate of taxation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Second, this principle would give parliament greater control over government spending and gov-

eminent waste. The government could no longer count upon inflation to ensure that a given tax structure would, in each year, place in its hands a greater percentage of the gross national product. The government would be under heavy pressure to economize. It would be collecting personal income taxes in terms of 1971 dollars but it would be paying its bills in terms of current dollars. Everybody concerned about government waste, everybody concerned about the government taking more of the GNP without anybody's permission, should enthusiastically support the kind of proposal I am putting forward. Clearly, this proposal would not only remove the vested interests of the government in inflation but would give the government a positive motivation to fight inflation.
As the leader of a government. I would implement the proposal fully, given the chance, as of January 1, 1973. The cost of living de-escalator would be applied to 1973 for a tax de-escalation in a proportion to be determined by Statistics Canada, on the basis of comparison between the cost of living for the 12 months terminating September 30, 1972, and the 12 months terminating September 30, 1971. For convenience of calculation, we would go to the nearest percentage point. Clearly, there would have to be discussions with the provinces. There is no doubt about that. There would have to be discussion in connection with their own problems associated with maintaining a single joint tax return. I think this would probably involve the negotiating of new tax agreements with the provinces rather than the standpat agreement of which the minister is so proud, and while we were negotiating these with the provinces we would make a real effort to get sensible integration between the capital gains tax and the succession duties of the provinces.
For the balance of 1972, we would adopt an interim arrangement. We propose to assume the cost of living in 1972 to be about 5 per cent higher than in 1971. There has already been a tax reduction of 3 per cent which came into effect as of last October. That means there is still 2 per cent to be taken care of now. I repeat we are assuming a 5 per cent increase in the cost of living, and there has been a tax reduction of 3 per cent. This would involve a cut of 4 per cent in tax rates for the last six months of 1972 which, I think, would involve about $160 million. This would mean that it would be an interim arrangement to be in effect this year. This would be fair to the taxpayers. It would encourage a feeling of fairness and, therefore, restraint in Canadian society. It would stimulate the Canadian economy, and thereby tend to cut down unemployment, rather than accept the massive degree of unemployment that the government is accepting. We are concerned about unemployment. We are concerned about inflation. We are concerned about the ever-growing percentage of the gross national product that the government is acquiring without any authorization. We are concerned about restoring parliamentary control over government taxation and government spending. We are concerned about government waste.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I have outlined, and I am afraid at rather great length, some specific, concrete and, I believe, effective measures for implementing this concern, for fighting unemployment, for removing the government's vested interest in inflation, for controlling the government's percentage of the GNP, for increasing par-
May 15, 1972

liamentary control over taxation and spending, as well as for putting real pressure on the government to eliminate waste. I will seize an early opportunity to satisfy the curiosity of the Secretary of State for External Affairs about some of these matters, about how we are going to encourage more Canadian investment in the Canadian economy. I will do this probably later in this debate, although we do not know how long this debate will be allowed to continue. I will do it probably after the vote on the amendment put forward by hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert).
I will outline further measures that should be adopted to create more employment through creation of new Canadian enterprises, through creation of pools of venture capital, and measures to enable Canadians to increase their control of the Canadian economy. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the ministers opposite will have to wait for the next exciting installment in order to learn this. I have said enough today to indicate how unresponsive the government is to the needs of the country at the present time. I have outlined some of the important measures which would be responsive to those needs, measures which a Progressive Conservative government would implement. I, therefore, ask all hon. members to support the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton West.
